sharedText: gathered … of every kind … into vessels … fish
reason: Not proposed by the machine and tempting enough that it should be recorded as considered and declined. Read Ether 2:1-2 straight through and three rare KJV items fall in Matthew's order: 'gathered together … of every kind' (“of every kind” occurs in exactly 2 KJV verses, 1 Chronicles 28:14 and Matthew 13:47), then a vessel prepared (“into vessels” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 13:48), then 'the fish of the waters'. Matthew 13:47-48 is the dragnet: 'a net, that was cast into the sea, and gathered of every kind: which, when it was full, they drew to shore, and sat down, and gathered the good into vessels, but cast the bad away.' Fish, of every kind, vessels — in that sequence, in one two-verse parable, and nowhere else in the KJV. It still fails, on referents. The Book of Mormon's 'of every kind' attaches to flocks gathered male and female, not to fish; its vessel is a water-tank for carrying live fish on a journey, not a sorting basket on a shore; and its fish are being preserved where Matthew's good fish are being selected and the rest thrown away. The parable is an image of the last judgment separating the righteous from the wicked, and Ether 2:1-3 is an inventory that separates nothing — the whole point of the manifest is that everything comes. The shared items are three, they are rare, and each is doing a different job in each text. The verses' real source is the ark manifest of Genesis 6:19-7:3, which is adjudicated as a link at 2:3.

The machine's top-ranked candidate for the verse (rarity 2.00, a five-word run) and pure artifact. Judges 14:7 is Samson going down to Timnath to talk with the Philistine woman he means to marry: 'And he went down, and talked with the woman; and she pleased Samson well.' Ether 2:4 is the Lord coming down into the valley of Nimrod and talking with the brother of Jared out of a cloud he cannot be seen through. The shared string is 'down, and talked with the', of which every word is connective; the run scores because English puts those five words in that order whenever anyone descends and speaks. Nothing else of the Samson narrative is anywhere near this chapter. The real source of the verse's descent-and-speech is the cloud theophany of Numbers 11:25 and Exodus 33:9, which is adjudicated as a link at 2:4.

A better temptation than the Samson row, because the shared element is not merely connective: both verses bring a people down into a named valley, and named valleys are not common. Joel 3:2 reads 'I will also gather all nations, and will bring them down into the valley of Jehoshaphat, and will plead with them there for my people and for my heritage Israel.' The senses are opposed at the load-bearing point. Joel's valley is the valley of decision (3:14), the nations are gathered into it to be judged and the sickle is put in because their wickedness is great; Ether's valley is a staging ground from which a favoured company departs before a judgment, and the Lord who comes down into it comes to give travel directions. Joel gathers the nations in; Ether sends one family out. The valley's name is also doing entirely different work in each — 'Jehoshaphat' is glossed by Joel as 'the LORD judgeth', 'Nimrod' is glossed by Ether as the mighty hunter of Genesis 10:9, and that gloss is where the verse's real borrowing lies (see the link at 2:1). Worth recording because the harvest-of-wrath imagery Joel 3:13 supplies does bear on this chapter — at 2:15, where 'fully ripe' is adjudicated to Revelation 14:18, which is itself rewriting Joel.

sharedText: (that quarter where there never had man been)
reason: A typological expectation with nothing under it, filed on the model of the Exodus 2:2 'goodly' entry in 1 Nephi. The Jaredites are sent 'into that quarter where there never had man been', and the KJV's formula for a place no man has occupied belongs almost entirely to two objects: the colt whereon never man sat (Mark 11:2, Luke 19:30) and the sepulchre wherein never man was laid (Luke 23:53, John 19:41). “never man” occurs in 5 KJV verses and four of them are those. The pull is real — a virgin land entered by a chosen remnant is a resurrection image, and this chapter will bury its travellers in the deep and raise them again at 2:24 — but the wording will not carry it. The Book of Mormon's construction is 'where there never had man been', which shares only the two commonest words of the KJV's 'wherein never man', and the Gospel formula is always about a receptacle prepared for a single sacred occupant, never about territory. Recorded so that a reader who feels the type is told the catalogue felt it too and declined it.

sharedText: it came to pass … that the Lord did bring
reason: 'The Lord did bring Jared and his brethren forth even to that great sea' against 'the LORD did bring the children of Israel out of the land of Egypt by their armies'. The five-word run is 'it came to pass … that the Lord did bring', and it is the exodus formula, which the Book of Mormon uses continuously and which the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 2:1 covers for 'and it came to pass'. The exodus framing of this journey is real and is catalogued where it has wording to stand on — at 2:5, where Deuteronomy 1:33's going-before, cloud and pitching of tents are reproduced, and at 2:23, where the pillar of fire is explicitly withheld. Exodus 12:51 adds nothing those rows do not have and its distinctive matter (the armies, the selfsame day, the land of Egypt) is absent. This entry also covers Joshua 1:1, which the machine returned twice in this chapter on 'it came to pass that the Lord', and Amos 7:2 at 2:4 on 'and it came to pass, that when they had'.

A five-word run and one of the register's better entries, because the coincidence is not in connective tissue but in a specified interval. Acts 5:7: 'And it was about the space of three hours after, when his wife, not knowing what was done, came in' — the three hours between Ananias's death and Sapphira's arrival, after which she lies to Peter and is carried out dead. Ether 2:14: three hours in which the Lord chastens the brother of Jared for four years of not calling on his name, at the end of which he is forgiven. Both intervals are three hours; both stand between a fault and its reckoning; and there the resemblance stops. In Acts the three hours are dead time whose only function is that Sapphira does not yet know, and the reckoning is a death sentence; in Ether the three hours are the chastening itself, and the reckoning is forgiveness within one verse. The KJV's other 'space of three' is months (Acts 19:8), which the machine also returned. Neither is a source. What the three hours in Ether 2:14 are doing is fixing the scale of a rebuke, and the KJV has no verse that does that.

sharedText: to call upon the name of the Lord
reason: An eight-word run, the longest in the verse, and it cannot bear a link because the phrase is stock in both corpora: “call upon the name of the Lord” occurs in 5 KJV verses (Genesis 4:26, Psalm 116:13, 116:17, Zephaniah 3:9, Romans 10:13) and the Book of Mormon uses it constantly. Recorded rather than passed over in silence because of where it falls. Genesis 4:26 is the primeval history's note that 'then began men to call upon the name of the LORD', and this chapter is saturated with Genesis 4-11 — Nimrod at 2:1, the ark manifest at 2:3, Genesis 6:3 quoted verbatim at 2:15, the ark's door and window at 2:17 and 2:23. A rebuke for NOT calling on the name of the Lord, delivered in a chapter working through Genesis in order, sitting next to the KJV verse that reports when men began to, is a pattern a careful reader would want to weigh. It does not survive the count: five KJV verses is not a source, and the Book of Mormon's own usage is dense enough that the phrase would be here whatever Genesis said. The chapter's Genesis dependence is catalogued where the wording is rare.

sharedText: in them there is no light
reason: Not a rejection but a cross-reference, of the kind ruled admissible at Mosiah 11:14. The brother of Jared's first complaint, 'in them there is no light', is the same six words as Isaiah 8:20's KJV singleton 'there is no light in them', in a different order. The link is written at 2:22, where the complaint is repeated in Isaiah's own word order — 'behold, there is no light in them' — because that is where the borrowing is demonstrable rather than merely present. A reader arriving at 2:19 and finding nothing should be sent three verses on rather than told there is no contact here; there is, and it is the same contact.

Considered and declined, and worth the entry because the coincidence is exact where it is exact. “dash them in pieces” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Psalm 2:9 — 'thou shalt break them with a rod of iron; thou shalt dash them in pieces like a potter's vessel' — and it is the KJV's only verse in which something is dashed in pieces AND is a vessel. Ether 2:23 is about vessels and uses 'dashed in pieces' in the same breath. But the grammar refuses it: what will be dashed in pieces in Ether is the windows, and the vessels are the thing the windows would be set into, so the two rare terms sit on opposite sides of the sentence from where Psalm 2 puts them. The senses are opposed as well — Psalm 2:9 is the Son shattering rebellious nations with an iron rod, Ether 2:23 is a shipwright's objection about glazing — and “dashed in pieces” itself occurs in 4 KJV verses (Exodus 15:6, Hosea 10:14, 13:16, Nahum 3:10), all of them massacres. There is no route from any of them to a window. The verse's real sources are Genesis 6:16 and Exodus 13:21, both adjudicated as links at 2:23.

A five-word run and the machine's third candidate for the verse: 'I will bring you up out of the affliction of Egypt unto the land of the Canaanites.' The words are right and the verse is not. Exodus 3:17's motion is up out of Egypt into Canaan, a geography with no sea in it and no depths; the run scores because 'I will bring you up' is a common divine promise. Ether 2:24's clause is 'I will bring you up again out of the depths of the sea', and its distinctive elements are 'again' and 'the depths of the sea', neither of which Exodus 3:17 has. Both are KJV singletons elsewhere — “from the depths of the sea” at Psalm 68:22, which is also a first-person promise of the Lord to bring his people back out of the sea, and “bring me up again” at Psalm 71:20. The link is written at 2:24 to Psalm 68:22 with Psalm 71:20 as composite.

The machine returned Matthew 20:32 at both 2:23 and 2:25 as the top candidate, on the four words 'What will ye that I'. Matthew's form is 'What will ye that I shall do unto you?' and the Book of Mormon's is 'What will ye that I should do' — 'should', not 'shall', which is Mark's. “that I should do unto thee” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Mark 10:51, the question put to blind Bartimaeus whose answer is 'that I might receive my sight'. The link is written at 2:23, the question's first occurrence, with Matthew 20:32 and Mark 10:36 recorded as composite because the Book of Mormon's plural 'ye' is theirs and its 'I should do' is Mark 10:51's. This entry sends a reader at 2:25 — where the question is asked a second time, and where the Lord finally completes it with 'that ye may have light' — to the adjudication at 2:23 rather than repeating it.
